title: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition

learn.hook: Thousands of farmers sell the same variety of wheat at a mandi. If one farmer asks ₹50 more per quintal, buyers simply walk to the next heap. That is perfect competition.
points: Large number of buyers and sellers: each is too small to influence the market price.
Homogeneous product: every firm's output is identical, so buyers have no reason to prefer one seller.
Free entry and exit: firms can enter or leave the industry without restrictions.
Perfect information: all buyers and sellers know the market price and product details.
Result: each firm is a price taker. It can sell any quantity at the market price, so it faces a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve.

example.q: A wheat farmer finds the market price is ₹2,300 per quintal. What happens if she charges (a) ₹2,350, (b) ₹2,250?
steps: (a) Buyers know the price and the wheat is identical, so they buy elsewhere: she sells nothing.
(b) She could sell all she wants at ₹2,300 anyway, so cutting price only lowers her revenue.
example.answer: She charges the market price of ₹2,300: she is a price taker.

learn.reallife: Agricultural produce like wheat or potatoes sold through mandis comes close to perfect competition; most other markets fall short of the ideal.

games.title: Match the feature to its effect
pairs: No single firm can affect price
Buyers do not prefer any seller
Firms earn only normal profit in the long run
Horizontal demand curve for the firm

games.title: Perfect competition
items: A perfectly competitive firm can set its own price.
It takes the market price as given.
The demand curve facing a perfectly competitive firm is horizontal.
It can sell any quantity at the market price.
Products of different firms are identical under perfect competition.
They are homogeneous.
Entry of new firms is restricted under perfect competition.
There is free entry and exit.
Each buyer and seller has perfect information about prices.
That is one of the features.

quiz.q: Under perfect competition, an individual firm is a:
quiz.explain: It is too small to influence price, so it accepts the market price.
steps: Under perfect competition each firm is tiny compared with the whole market.
It cannot influence the market price, so it accepts it.
A firm that accepts the given price is a price taker.
Monopolists and price makers set prices → 'Price taker'.
Answer: Price taker
quiz.mistake: Thinks firms always set prices

quiz.q: The demand curve faced by a perfectly competitive firm is:
quiz.explain: At the market price it can sell any quantity; at a higher price, nothing.
steps: At the market price the firm can sell any quantity it wants.
At a higher price it sells nothing, since identical goods are available elsewhere.
So its demand curve is flat at the market price.
It is horizontal (perfectly elastic).
Answer: Horizontal (perfectly elastic)
quiz.mistake: Confuses the firm's demand curve with the market demand curve

quiz.q: Which is NOT a feature of perfect competition?
options: Large number of buyers and sellers
quiz.explain: With identical products and perfect information, advertising serves no purpose.
steps: Features: many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, free entry and exit, perfect information.
With identical products and perfect information, advertising serves no purpose.
So heavy advertising by each firm is not a feature.
Answer: Heavy advertising by each firm
quiz.mistake: Confuses perfect competition with other market forms

quiz.q: If a perfectly competitive firm raises its price above the market price, it will:
quiz.explain: Buyers can buy the identical product elsewhere at the market price.
steps: The product is identical across all firms.
If one firm charges more, buyers buy from others at the market price.
So it loses all its buyers.
It will sell nothing.
Answer: Sell nothing
quiz.mistake: Ignores the role of homogeneous products

quiz.q: The price elasticity of demand facing a perfectly competitive firm is:
quiz.explain: A horizontal demand curve is perfectly elastic.
steps: The firm's demand curve is horizontal.
A horizontal demand curve means even a tiny price rise cuts sales to zero.
Rule: horizontal demand curve = perfectly elastic.
So the elasticity is infinite.
Answer: Infinite
quiz.mistake: Confuses perfectly elastic with perfectly inelastic

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker.
Reason (R): Each firm supplies a very small share of total market output of a homogeneous product.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Being tiny and identical to others, a firm cannot influence price.
steps: A: a perfectly competitive firm is a price taker → true.
R: each firm supplies a tiny share of total output of a homogeneous product → true.
Being tiny and identical to others, a firm cannot influence price.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Knows the conclusion but not the reason

quiz.q: Free entry and exit under perfect competition ensures that in the long run firms earn:
quiz.explain: New entrants wipe out extra profits; exits remove losses.
steps: If firms earn super-normal profit, new firms enter and price falls.
If firms make losses, some leave and price rises.
This continues until only normal profit remains.
So in the long run firms earn only normal profit.
Answer: Only normal profit
quiz.mistake: Thinks profits stay high

quiz.q: A market price of ₹40 prevails. A perfectly competitive firm sells 150 units. What is its total revenue?
steps: Rule: TR = p × q.
So total revenue = ₹6,000.
Answer: ₹6,000
quiz.mistake: Adds price and quantity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why can't one berry seller in a huge market charge more than the others? Teach me perfect competition!'
teach.praise: Tweet! With many sellers of identical berries and perfect information, each seller must take the market price!
teach.nudge: Good! But why can't one seller charge more? Think about the products and how many sellers there are.

revise.summary: Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit, and perfect information. So each firm is a price taker facing a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve.
focus: List the features of perfect competition
Explain why a firm is a price taker
Know the shape and elasticity of the firm's demand curve
Know that free entry and exit leave only normal profit in the long run
remember: Features: many buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect information
Firm's demand curve: horizontal, perfectly elastic (e_D infinite)
traps: Don't confuse the firm's horizontal demand curve with the market demand curve
A firm that charges above the market price sells nothing
Heavy advertising is not a feature of perfect competition

learn.hook: A candle maker sells boxes at the market price of ₹10. Every box adds exactly ₹10 to revenue, so her revenue curves are as simple as they get.
points: TR = p × q. With a constant market price, TR is a straight line through the origin whose slope equals the price.
AR = TR/q = p and MR = ΔTR/Δq = p for a price taker.
So the firm's price line = AR = MR = its demand curve: one horizontal line at the market price.
If the market price rises, the TR line becomes steeper and the AR = MR line shifts up.

example.q: Candle boxes sell at ₹10. Find TR and MR for 1 to 5 boxes.
steps: MR = 10 for every box
AR = 10 for every quantity
example.answer: TR rises by ₹10 per box; AR = MR = ₹10.

learn.reallife: A farmer selling tomatoes at a mandi where the day's price is ₹20 per kg earns ₹20 on every extra kg: her MR equals the price.

items.q: Slope of TR line when p = 15?

games.title: Price line facts
items: For a price taker, AR = MR = price.
Every unit sells at the same market price.
The TR curve of a price taker passes through the origin.
Zero output gives zero revenue.
The slope of the TR line equals the market price.
TR rises by p for each unit.
A rise in the market price makes the TR line flatter.
It makes the TR line steeper.
A price taker's demand curve slopes downward.
It is horizontal at the market price.

quiz.q: For a perfectly competitive firm, the TR curve is:
options: A straight line through the origin with slope equal to price
quiz.explain: TR = p × q with constant p.
steps: For a price taker, TR = p × q with p constant.
TR = 0 at q = 0 and rises by p for each extra unit.
So the TR curve is a straight line through the origin.
Its slope equals the price.
Answer: A straight line through the origin with slope equal to price
quiz.mistake: Confuses TR with AR

quiz.q: For a price-taking firm, which of these is equal to the market price?
quiz.explain: Every unit sells at p, so AR = MR = p.
steps: Every unit is sold at the market price p.
AR = TR/q = p.
MR = extra revenue from one more unit = p.
So both AR and MR equal the market price.
Answer: Both AR and MR
quiz.mistake: Thinks only AR equals price

quiz.q: Candle boxes sell at ₹10 each. What is TR from 7 boxes?
steps: Rule: TR = p × q.
So TR = ₹70.
Answer: ₹70
quiz.mistake: Adds price and quantity

quiz.q: A firm's TR rises from ₹150 to ₹165 when it sells one more unit. If it is a price taker, what is the market price?
quiz.explain: MR = 165 − 150 = 15, and for a price taker MR = p.
steps: For a price taker, MR = price.
So the market price = ₹15.
₹165 and ₹150 are TR figures, not the price.
Answer: ₹15
quiz.mistake: Reads the TR value as the price

quiz.q: The slope of the TR curve of a price-taking firm when the price is ₹25 is:
quiz.explain: TR rises by ₹25 per unit sold.
steps: Slope of TR = extra TR from one more unit = MR.
For a price taker, MR = price = ₹25.
So TR rises by ₹25 per unit sold.
Slope = 25.
Answer: 25
quiz.mistake: Thinks a straight line through the origin always has slope 1

quiz.q: The firm's demand curve under perfect competition is the same as its:
options: AR and MR curve (the price line)
quiz.explain: All are the horizontal line at the market price.
steps: The firm's demand curve is horizontal at the market price.
AR = MR = p, so the AR and MR curves are that same horizontal line.
MC, TR and AC curves have other shapes.
So the demand curve is the AR and MR curve (the price line).
Answer: AR and MR curve (the price line)
quiz.mistake: Confuses demand with cost curves

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For a price-taking firm, MR equals AR.
Reason (R): Selling an extra unit does not require lowering the price on any unit.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With a fixed price, each extra unit adds exactly p to revenue.
steps: A: for a price-taking firm, MR equals AR → true.
R: selling an extra unit does not require lowering price on any unit → true.
With a fixed price, each extra unit adds exactly p, so MR = p = AR.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks MR must be less than AR

quiz.q: The market price rises from ₹10 to ₹12. What happens to a price taker's TR at 50 units?
quiz.explain: TR rises from 500 to 600, an increase of ₹100.
steps: Rise = 100
Answer: Rises by ₹100
quiz.mistake: Applies the price change to one unit only

teach.ask: Gappu sells berry boxes at ₹5 each in a huge market. 'What do my TR, AR and MR look like on a graph?'
teach.praise: Tweet! TR is a straight line from the origin, and AR = MR = ₹5 is a horizontal price line!
teach.nudge: Good! Is TR curved or straight? And how do AR and MR compare with the price?

revise.summary: For a price-taking firm, TR is a straight line through the origin with slope equal to the price, and AR = MR = price. Its price line, AR, MR and demand curve are one horizontal line.
focus: Calculate TR, AR and MR for a price taker
Find the market price from a change in TR
Explain why AR = MR for a price taker
remember: TR = p × q: a straight line through the origin with slope = price
Price line = AR = MR = demand curve of the firm
traps: The slope of the TR line is the price, not always 1
MR is not less than AR for a price taker: they are equal
Don't read the TR value as the price

learn.hook: Should a firm stop producing when price equals marginal cost? Only if three conditions hold, and the third tells it when to shut down altogether.
points: Profit (π) = TR − TC. A firm chooses output to make profit as large as possible.
Condition 1: price = marginal cost (p = MC, i.e. MR = MC). If p > MC, one more unit adds to profit; if p < MC, cutting output raises profit.
Condition 2: MC must be non-decreasing (rising) at that output. Where MC is falling and equals p, producing more would still raise profit.
Condition 3 (short run): price must be at least minimum AVC. If p < min AVC, the firm should shut down; its loss is then only the TFC.
Condition 3 (long run): price must be at least minimum LRAC; otherwise the firm exits the industry.

example.q: A firm's MC equals the price of ₹20 at two outputs: 10 units (MC falling) and 40 units (MC rising). At 40 units AVC = ₹16. What output should it choose?
steps: At 10 units MC is falling: Condition 2 fails.
At 40 units MC is rising: Condition 2 holds.
Price ₹20 ≥ AVC ₹16: Condition 3 holds.

learn.reallife: Sugar mills crush cane only when the sugar price covers their variable costs (cane, power, wages); otherwise they stay shut for the season.

games.title: Checking the profit-maximising output
items: Find the outputs where p = MC
Keep only the output where MC is rising
Check that p ≥ minimum AVC (short run)
If yes, produce that output; if not, shut down

games.title: Produce or shut down (short run)?
items: p = ₹30, min AVC = ₹25
p = ₹18, min AVC = ₹20
p = ₹40, min AVC = ₹40
p = ₹12, min AVC = ₹15
p below min AVC but above AFC
p above min AVC but below min AC

quiz.q: The first condition for profit maximisation of a price-taking firm is:
quiz.explain: Output is set where the price equals marginal cost.
steps: Profit is maximised where producing one more unit adds as much to revenue as to cost.
For a price taker, extra revenue per unit = p.
So output is set where p = MC.
That is the first condition (MC must also be rising).
Answer: p = MC
quiz.mistake: Confuses profit maximisation with break-even

quiz.q: Why must MC be rising at the profit-maximising output?
options: If MC is falling where p = MC, producing a little more would add to profit
quiz.explain: Beyond that point p > MC, so profit is not yet maximised.
steps: Suppose p = MC where MC is falling.
Producing a little more, MC falls below p, so each extra unit adds more revenue than cost.
So profit could still rise, and that point is not a maximum.
Hence MC must be rising at the profit-maximising output.
Answer: If MC is falling where p = MC, producing a little more would add to profit
quiz.mistake: Thinks any point where p = MC is optimal

quiz.q: In the short run, a firm should shut down if the price is less than:
quiz.explain: Below minimum AVC, it cannot even cover variable costs.
steps: If price is below minimum AVC, the firm cannot cover even its variable costs.
Producing would then lose more than TFC.
Shutting down limits the loss to TFC.
So it should shut down if price < minimum AVC.
Answer: Minimum AVC
quiz.mistake: Uses the long-run condition (minimum AC)

quiz.q: A firm with TFC = ₹500 shuts down in the short run. What is its loss?
quiz.explain: With zero output, TR = 0 and TC = TFC, so the loss equals TFC.
steps: If it shuts down, output = 0 → TR = 0 and TVC = 0.
TC = TFC = ₹500.
Loss = TC − TR = 500 − 0.
So the loss = ₹500 (equal to TFC).
Answer: ₹500
quiz.mistake: Thinks shutting down removes all losses

quiz.q: In the long run, a perfectly competitive firm stays in the industry only if price is at least:
quiz.explain: In the long run all costs must be covered.
steps: In the long run all costs are variable and must be covered.
Price must at least equal the lowest long-run average cost.
Otherwise the firm leaves the industry.
So price must be at least minimum LRAC.
Answer: Minimum LRAC
quiz.mistake: Uses the short-run shut-down rule

quiz.q: At the current output, p = ₹50 and MC = ₹42 (MC rising). To raise profit the firm should:
quiz.explain: Each extra unit adds ₹50 of revenue but only about ₹42 of cost.
steps: The next unit adds ₹50 to revenue but only about ₹42 to cost.
So producing more raises profit.
The firm should increase output (until p = MC).
Answer: Increase output
quiz.mistake: Reverses the MR–MC rule

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A firm may continue producing in the short run even when it makes a loss.
Reason (R): If the price covers AVC, producing keeps the loss smaller than TFC.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Covering variable cost and part of fixed cost beats losing all of TFC.
steps: A: a firm may keep producing in the short run even at a loss → true.
R: if price covers AVC, producing keeps the loss smaller than TFC → true.
Covering variable cost and part of fixed cost beats losing all of TFC.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks a loss-making firm must close at once

quiz.q: p = ₹30, and at the output where p = MC (MC rising), AVC = ₹28 and AC = ₹33. In the short run the firm should:
options: Produce, since p ≥ AVC, accepting a small loss
quiz.explain: Price covers AVC (₹30 > ₹28), so producing minimises the loss.
steps: Compare price with AVC: p = ₹30 ≥ AVC = ₹28 → produce.
p = ₹30 < AC = ₹33 → there is a small loss.
Loss per unit = 33 − 30 = ₹3, smaller than if it shut down and lost all fixed cost.
So produce, since p ≥ AVC, accepting a small loss.
Answer: Produce, since p ≥ AVC, accepting a small loss
quiz.mistake: Applies the long-run rule in the short run

teach.ask: Gappu's nest business: price ₹20, MC equals ₹20 at 8 nests (rising), AVC = ₹15. 'Should I make 8 nests?'
teach.praise: Tweet! p = MC at 8 nests, MC is rising and the price covers AVC, so 8 nests maximise profit!
teach.nudge: Good! Is MC rising there? And does the price at least cover my average variable cost?

revise.summary: A price-taking firm maximises profit where p = MC, with MC rising, and price at least minimum AVC in the short run (minimum LRAC in the long run). Below minimum AVC it shuts down and loses only TFC.
focus: State the three conditions for profit maximisation
Explain why MC must be rising
Apply the short-run shut-down rule and the long-run exit rule
Decide whether to raise or cut output when p ≠ MC
remember: Profit π = TR − TC
Conditions: p = MC; MC non-decreasing; p ≥ min AVC (short run), p ≥ min LRAC (long run)
On shut-down the loss is only TFC
traps: Not every point where p = MC is optimal: MC must be rising
Don't use minimum AC as the short-run shut-down rule: it is minimum AVC
Shutting down does not remove all losses: TFC is still lost

topics.title: Profit and loss: graphs and numericals

learn.hook: On a graph, profit is literally a rectangle: its height is price minus average cost, and its width is output. Draw it right and you can read profit at a glance.
points: Graph: the firm produces q0 where the horizontal price line meets the rising SMC. Profit (or loss) = (p − SAC at q0) × q0.
If p > SAC at q0: super-normal profit, shown by the rectangle between price and SAC. If p < SAC but p ≥ AVC: a loss rectangle, but the firm still produces in the short run.
From a table: profit = TR − TC at each output; choose the output with the highest profit. Equivalently, keep producing while MC ≤ p.
Check: at the chosen output, MC of the next unit should exceed the price.

example.q: Price ₹10. TC at q = 0 to 6: 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47. Find the profit-maximising output.
example.answer: q = 5, profit ₹14 (MC of the 6th unit, ₹11, exceeds the price).

learn.reallife: A hand-pump manufacturer in Ludhiana that checks profit at each output level is doing exactly this table analysis.

games.title: Reading profit from a graph
items: Draw the horizontal price line
Find q0 where price meets rising SMC
Read SAC at q0
Profit = (price − SAC) × q0

quiz.q: Price = ₹20, output = 100 units, SAC at that output = ₹15. What is the profit?
steps: Profit per unit = 20 − 15 = 5
Answer: ₹500
quiz.mistake: Uses TR or TC instead of the difference

quiz.q: Price = ₹12, output = 80, SAC = ₹15, AVC = ₹10. What is the loss, and should the firm produce in the short run?
options: Loss ₹240; no, it must shut down
Loss ₹240; yes, since price covers AVC
quiz.explain: Loss = (15 − 12) × 80 = ₹240. Price (₹12) > AVC (₹10), so producing is better than shutting down.
steps: Price ₹12 > AVC ₹10, so variable cost is covered with something to spare.
So: loss ₹240; yes, produce, since price covers AVC.
Answer: Loss ₹240; yes, since price covers AVC
quiz.mistake: Forgets to compare price with AVC

quiz.q: Price ₹10. TC for q = 0 to 6: 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47. What is the profit-maximising output?
steps: The largest profit is ₹14.
It occurs at q = 5.
Answer: 5
quiz.mistake: Picks the largest output

quiz.q: Using the same table (p = ₹10; TC 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47 for q = 0–6), what is the maximum profit?
quiz.explain: At q = 5: TR = 50, TC = 36, profit = ₹14.
steps: Profit-maximising output (from the table) is q = 5.
So maximum profit = ₹14.
Answer: ₹14
quiz.mistake: Reads TR instead of profit

quiz.q: Price ₹10; TC for q = 0 to 6 is 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47. What is MC of the 6th unit, and why does the firm not produce it?
quiz.explain: MC6 = 47 − 36 = 11 > 10, so the 6th unit reduces profit.
steps: Price = ₹10.
MC (₹11) > price (₹10), so the 6th unit adds more to cost than to revenue.
So MC = ₹11; the firm does not produce it because it exceeds the price.
Answer: ₹11; it exceeds the price of ₹10
quiz.mistake: Uses TC instead of MC

quiz.q: On a cost–revenue diagram, the profit of a firm is shown by a rectangle whose height is:
options: Price minus SAC at the chosen output
quiz.explain: Profit per unit (p − SAC) times output gives the rectangle's area.
steps: Profit = (p − SAC) × q.
On the diagram, q is the width of the rectangle.
So its height is profit per unit, p − SAC at the chosen output.
Answer: Price minus SAC at the chosen output
quiz.mistake: Uses MC instead of AC for per-unit profit

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): When price equals SAC at the chosen output, the firm earns zero economic profit.
Reason (R): TR then exactly equals TC, which already includes normal profit.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: p = SAC means TR = TC, so only normal profit is earned.
steps: A: when p = SAC at the chosen output, economic profit is zero → true.
R: TR then equals TC, which already includes normal profit → true.
p = SAC gives TR = TC, so only normal profit is earned.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero economic profit means the owner earns nothing

quiz.q: A firm sells 60 units at ₹25. TC is ₹1,350. What is its profit?
steps: So profit = ₹150.
Answer: ₹150
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order

teach.ask: Gappu's price is ₹8 per nest, he makes 50 nests, and his average cost is ₹6. 'How much profit? Can I show it on a graph?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Profit = (8 − 6) × 50 = ₹100, the rectangle between the price line and the AC curve!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the profit on each nest? Then multiply by what?

revise.summary: The firm produces where the price line meets the rising SMC. Profit or loss = (p − SAC) × output; from a table, choose the output with the highest TR − TC.

topics.title: The firm's supply curve, shut-down point and normal profit

learn.hook: Plot how much a firm produces at every price and you've drawn its supply curve. Surprise: it's just a piece of its marginal cost curve.
points: Short-run supply curve of a firm: the rising part of the SMC curve from minimum AVC upward. At prices below minimum AVC, output is zero.
Long-run supply curve: the rising part of the LRMC curve from minimum LRAC upward; below minimum LRAC, output is zero.
Shut-down point: in the short run, the point of minimum AVC (where SMC cuts AVC); in the long run, minimum LRAC.
Normal profit: the minimum profit needed to keep the firm in business. It is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur (the return from the next best alternative) and is counted as part of cost.
Super-normal profit: profit above normal profit. Break-even point: where price = minimum AC, so the firm earns only normal profit (zero economic profit).

example.q: A firm's minimum AVC is ₹20 and minimum AC is ₹30. What does it do at prices of ₹15, ₹25 and ₹40?
steps: ₹15 < min AVC: shut down (output 0).
₹25: between min AVC and min AC: produces where p = SMC, with a loss smaller than TFC.
₹40 > min AC: produces where p = SMC and earns super-normal profit.
example.answer: Shut down at ₹15; produce at a loss at ₹25; produce with super-normal profit at ₹40.

learn.reallife: A software engineer who leaves a ₹15 lakh job to start a firm counts that ₹15 lakh as normal profit: her opportunity cost.

It shuts down.
Normal profit is included in the cost of production.
It is the entrepreneur's opportunity cost.
At the break-even point the firm earns super-normal profit.
It earns only normal profit.
The short-run supply curve is the entire SMC curve.
Only the rising part above minimum AVC.
Opportunity cost is the return from the next best alternative use.

quiz.q: The short-run supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm is:
options: The rising part of SMC above minimum AVC
quiz.explain: At each price above minimum AVC, the firm produces where p = rising SMC.
steps: At each price, the firm produces where p = rising SMC.
Below minimum AVC it shuts down and supplies nothing.
So only the rising SMC above minimum AVC shows quantity supplied.
That part is the short-run supply curve.
Answer: The rising part of SMC above minimum AVC
quiz.mistake: Includes the falling part of SMC

quiz.q: The short-run shut-down point of a firm is where price equals:
quiz.explain: Below minimum AVC, producing loses more than shutting down.
steps: If price is below minimum AVC, the firm loses more by producing than by shutting down.
At exactly minimum AVC, it is just indifferent.
That point is the shut-down point.
So price = minimum AVC.
Answer: Minimum AVC
quiz.mistake: Confuses shut-down with break-even

quiz.q: Normal profit is:
options: The minimum profit needed to keep the firm in the industry
quiz.explain: It is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur, counted as cost.
steps: Normal profit is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur.
It is the minimum profit needed to keep the firm in the industry.
It is counted as part of cost, so it is not profit above all costs.
Answer: The minimum profit needed to keep the firm in the industry
quiz.mistake: Thinks normal profit is extra profit

quiz.q: The break-even point is where:
quiz.explain: TR = TC, so the firm earns only normal profit.
steps: Break-even means TR = TC.
Per unit, this is price = AC; it happens at the lowest point of AC.
Then the firm earns only normal profit.
So break-even is where price = minimum AC.
Answer: Price = minimum AC
quiz.mistake: Mixes up break-even and shut-down points

quiz.q: Minimum AVC is ₹20 and minimum AC is ₹30. At a price of ₹25, the firm in the short run will:
options: Produce at a loss smaller than TFC
quiz.explain: Price covers AVC but not AC, so it produces and limits its loss.
steps: p = ₹25 > minimum AVC (₹20) → variable costs are covered, so produce.
p = ₹25 < minimum AC (₹30) → not all costs are covered, so there is a loss.
Producing covers part of fixed cost, so the loss is less than TFC.
So it produces at a loss smaller than TFC.
Answer: Produce at a loss smaller than TFC
quiz.mistake: Thinks any loss means shutting down

quiz.q: A teacher earning ₹60,000 a month quits to open a coaching centre. The opportunity cost of her own time is:
quiz.explain: The salary she gives up is her next best alternative.
steps: Opportunity cost = the value of the next best alternative given up.
By opening the centre she gives up her salary of ₹60,000 a month.
Rent and fees are other costs and revenues, not her time's opportunity cost.
So it is ₹60,000 a month.
Answer: ₹60,000 a month
quiz.mistake: Thinks opportunity cost means money actually spent

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A firm earning only normal profit will remain in the industry.
Reason (R): Normal profit covers the entrepreneur's opportunity cost.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since she earns as much as in her next best option, she has no reason to leave.
steps: A: a firm earning only normal profit will remain in the industry → true.
R: normal profit covers the entrepreneur's opportunity cost → true.
She earns as much as in her next best option, so she has no reason to leave.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero economic profit means the firm should leave

quiz.q: Price is ₹45 and minimum AC is ₹30. At the profit-maximising output the firm earns:
quiz.explain: Price above minimum AC means profit above normal.
steps: Price ₹45 > minimum AC ₹30.
So at the best output, revenue per unit exceeds cost per unit.
Profit above normal profit is super-normal profit.
So the firm earns super-normal profit.
Answer: Super-normal profit
quiz.mistake: Confuses super-normal and normal profit

teach.ask: Gappu's minimum AVC is ₹6 and minimum AC is ₹9. 'At what prices do I supply nests? What is my supply curve?'
teach.praise: Tweet! My supply curve is the rising MC above minimum AVC (₹6); below ₹6 I shut down, and at ₹9 I break even!
teach.nudge: Good! Below which price will I make nothing? Which part of the MC curve is my supply curve?

revise.summary: A firm's short-run supply curve is the rising part of SMC above minimum AVC; its long-run supply curve is the rising part of LRMC above minimum LRAC. Normal profit is the entrepreneur's opportunity cost, counted as cost.
focus: Define the short-run and long-run supply curves
Distinguish the shut-down point from the break-even point
Define normal and super-normal profit
Decide a firm's action at different prices
remember: Short-run shut-down point: minimum AVC; long-run: minimum LRAC
Break-even point: price = minimum AC (only normal profit)
Normal profit: the minimum profit to keep the firm in business, the entrepreneur's opportunity cost
traps: Don't include the falling part of SMC in the supply curve
Don't mix up the shut-down point (min AVC) with break-even (min AC)
Normal profit is not extra profit; zero economic profit does not mean the firm should leave

learn.hook: A new drip-irrigation technique cuts a farmer's cost per kg; a hike in diesel prices raises it. Each pushes the supply curve in a different direction.
points: Supply schedule: quantities a firm is willing to sell at different prices. Law of supply: other things equal, quantity supplied rises with price.
Movement along the supply curve: caused by a change in the good's own price (extension or contraction of supply). Shift: caused by other factors.
Technological progress lowers MC, shifting the supply curve to the right.
A rise in input prices (wages, raw materials, fuel) raises MC, shifting supply to the left.
A unit (per-unit) tax raises the firm's MC by the amount of the tax, shifting supply to the left (upward by the tax).

example.q: A firm supplies 100 units at ₹20. The government imposes a tax of ₹4 per unit. At what price will it now supply 100 units?
steps: The tax raises MC by ₹4 at every output.
To supply 100 units it now needs ₹20 + ₹4.
example.answer: ₹24; the supply curve shifts up (left) by ₹4.

learn.reallife: When CNG prices rise, auto-rickshaw operators' costs rise; at any given fare fewer rides are supplied: a leftward shift of supply.

games.title: Effect on supply curve

Rise in wages

games.title: Supply determinants
items: A unit tax shifts the supply curve to the left.
It raises MC by the tax.
A rise in the good's own price shifts the supply curve to the right.
It causes a movement along the curve.
Technological progress lowers MC.
More output from the same inputs.
Higher input prices increase supply.
They raise MC and decrease supply.
The law of supply says quantity supplied rises with price, other things equal.
A positive price–quantity relation.

quiz.q: Technological progress in production will:
options: Shift the supply curve to the left
Cause a movement along the supply curve
Shift the supply curve to the right
quiz.explain: Lower MC means more is supplied at every price.
steps: Better technology lowers the cost of producing each unit (lower MC).
So the firm supplies more at every price.
More at every price is a rightward shift.
Answer: Shift the supply curve to the right
quiz.mistake: Thinks technology only affects demand

quiz.q: A rise in the price of an input used by a firm will:
options: Increase quantity supplied along the curve
quiz.explain: Higher MC reduces the quantity supplied at every price.
steps: A dearer input raises the firm's marginal cost.
So it supplies less at every price.
Less at every price is a leftward shift.
Answer: Shift supply to the left
quiz.mistake: Confuses input prices with output price

quiz.q: A unit tax of ₹5 is imposed. A firm previously supplied 200 units at ₹30. At what price will it supply 200 units now?
quiz.explain: MC rises by ₹5 at every output, so it needs ₹35.
steps: A unit tax of ₹5 raises MC by ₹5 at every output.
Before the tax, 200 units were supplied at ₹30.
Now the firm needs ₹30 + ₹5 = ₹35 to supply 200 units.
So the price = ₹35.
Answer: ₹35
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the tax

quiz.q: A rise in the good's own price leads to:
options: An extension (movement up) along the supply curve
quiz.explain: Own-price changes move along the curve.
steps: A change in the good's own price moves along the same supply curve.
A price rise → more is supplied → movement up the curve.
Shifts happen only for non-price factors.
So it is an extension (movement up) along the supply curve.
Answer: An extension (movement up) along the supply curve
quiz.mistake: Confuses movement with shift

quiz.q: Which of these causes a leftward shift of a firm's supply curve?
quiz.explain: A unit tax raises the firm's marginal cost.
steps: A leftward shift means less supplied at every price, usually from higher costs.
A unit tax raises the firm's MC.
Subsidies, cheaper inputs and better technology lower MC → rightward shift.
So a unit tax shifts supply to the left.
Answer: Imposition of a unit tax
quiz.mistake: Picks a cost-reducing factor

quiz.q: Supply schedule: p = ₹10 → 40 units, ₹12 → 50 units, ₹14 → 60 units. How many extra units are supplied for each ₹2 rise in price?
quiz.explain: Quantity rises by 10 units for each ₹2 increase.
steps: ₹10 → ₹12: quantity 40 → 50, a rise of 10.
₹12 → ₹14: quantity 50 → 60, a rise of 10.
Each ₹2 rise adds the same amount.
So 10 extra units per ₹2 rise.
Answer: 10
quiz.mistake: Divides wrong quantities

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A unit tax shifts the supply curve upward by the amount of the tax.
Reason (R): The tax adds a fixed amount to the cost of producing every unit.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: MC at every output rises by the tax, so the curve moves up by that amount.
steps: A: a unit tax shifts the supply curve up by the amount of the tax → true.
R: the tax adds a fixed amount to the cost of every unit → true.
MC at every output rises by the tax, so the curve moves up by exactly that amount.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks a tax affects only demand

quiz.q: 'Increase in supply' refers to:
options: A movement up along the supply curve
A rise in the good's price
A rightward shift of the supply curve
quiz.explain: More is supplied at every price due to a non-price factor.
steps: 'Increase in supply' means more is supplied at every price.
This is caused by a non-price factor (e.g. better technology).
On the graph it is a rightward shift of the supply curve.
A movement up the curve is an 'extension', not an increase.
Answer: A rightward shift of the supply curve
quiz.mistake: Uses 'increase in supply' for an own-price effect

teach.ask: Gappu's twig price rose and a new nest-weaving trick was invented in the same week. 'What happens to my supply curve?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Costlier twigs shift supply left, the new technique shifts it right. Both work through MC!
teach.nudge: Good! How does each change affect my marginal cost? Which way does each one shift supply?

revise.summary: By the law of supply, quantity supplied rises with price, other things equal. Own-price changes move along the supply curve; technology, input prices and unit taxes shift it.
focus: Distinguish movements along and shifts of the supply curve
Predict the effect of technology, input prices and unit taxes on supply
Find the new supply price after a unit tax
remember: Technological progress lowers MC: supply shifts right
Higher input prices raise MC: supply shifts left
A unit tax raises MC by the tax: supply shifts left (upward by the tax)
traps: A rise in own price causes extension along the curve, not a shift
Don't subtract the tax: the required price rises by the tax
'Increase in supply' means a rightward shift, not an own-price effect

learn.hook: Two dairy farms: one starts selling milk at ₹10 a litre, the other only at ₹15. Add their supplies and the market supply curve gets a kink at ₹15.
points: Market supply is the horizontal summation of the supply curves of all firms: at each price, add the quantities supplied.
If firms have different shut-down prices, the market supply curve has kinks where each new firm starts producing.
Example: s1 = p − 10 for p ≥ 10 (0 below); s2 = p − 15 for p ≥ 15 (0 below). Market: 0 for p < 10; p − 10 for 10 ≤ p < 15; 2p − 25 for p ≥ 15.
With n identical firms each supplying s(p), market supply = n × s(p).
An increase in the number of firms shifts the market supply curve to the right; a decrease shifts it to the left.

example.q: s1 = p − 10 (p ≥ 10) and s2 = p − 15 (p ≥ 15). Find market supply at p = 12 and p = 20.
steps: p = 12: s1 = 2, s2 = 0 (below 15) → market = 2

learn.reallife: When many new solar-panel makers entered India's market, the market supply of panels shifted right at every price.

games.title: Market supply sprint (s1 = p − 10 for p ≥ 10; s2 = p − 15 for p ≥ 15)

items.q: 100 identical firms, each s = p − 5. Market at p = 8?

games.title: Market supply facts
items: Market supply is obtained by adding quantities supplied by all firms at each price.
Horizontal summation.
Different shut-down prices cause kinks in market supply.
A firm joins the market only above its shut-down price.
Entry of new firms shifts market supply to the left.
It shifts it to the right.
Market supply of 50 identical firms is 50 times one firm's supply.
At each price.
Market supply is found by adding prices vertically.
Quantities are added horizontally at each price.

quiz.q: Market supply is the:
options: Vertical summation of firms' supply curves
Horizontal summation of firms' supply curves
quiz.explain: At each price, quantities supplied by all firms are added.
steps: Market supply = total quantity supplied by all firms at each price.
So at each price we add the quantities of all firms.
Adding quantities at the same price is horizontal summation.
Answer: Horizontal summation of firms' supply curves
quiz.mistake: Adds prices instead of quantities

quiz.q: s1 = p − 10 for p ≥ 10 (0 otherwise) and s2 = p − 15 for p ≥ 15 (0 otherwise). What is market supply at p = ₹20?
steps: Market supply = 10 + 5.
= 15 units.
Answer: 15
quiz.mistake: Uses only one firm

quiz.q: Using the same firms, what is market supply at p = ₹12?
quiz.explain: s1 = 2; firm 2 does not produce below ₹15, so s2 = 0.
steps: Firm 2 needs p ≥ 15, so at ₹12 it produces 0.
Market supply = 2 + 0.
= 2 units (not −1).
Answer: 2
quiz.mistake: Includes a negative quantity for firm 2

quiz.q: Why does the market supply curve of these two firms have a kink at ₹15?
options: Firm 2 starts producing only at ₹15, so above ₹15 quantity rises twice as fast as price rises
quiz.explain: Beyond ₹15 both firms respond to price, so quantity rises twice as fast.
steps: Below ₹15 only firm 1 produces, so quantity rises 1 unit per ₹1.
From ₹15, firm 2 also starts producing.
Above ₹15 both firms respond, so quantity rises 2 units per ₹1.
That change at ₹15 creates the kink.
Answer: Firm 2 starts producing only at ₹15, so above ₹15 quantity rises twice as fast as price rises
quiz.mistake: Does not link kinks to shut-down prices

quiz.q: There are 50 identical firms, each with supply s = 2p − 10 for p ≥ 5. What is market supply at p = ₹10?
quiz.explain: Each firm supplies 2 × 10 − 10 = 10; 50 firms supply 500.
steps: Each firm at p = ₹10: s = 2 × 10 − 10 = 10 units.
Number of firms = 50.
Market supply = 50 × 10.
= 500 units.
Answer: 500
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by the number of firms

quiz.q: An increase in the number of firms in a market will:
options: Shift the market supply curve to the right
quiz.explain: More firms supply more at every price.
steps: Market supply adds up the supply of all firms.
More firms → more is supplied at every price.
More at every price = a rightward shift.
So the market supply curve shifts to the right.
Answer: Shift the market supply curve to the right
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of firms affects only price

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The market supply curve is flatter than each firm's supply curve when firms are identical.
Reason (R): At each price, market quantity is the sum of all firms' quantities, so it responds more in quantity to a price change.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Adding n identical curves horizontally multiplies the quantity response by n.
steps: A: market supply is flatter than each identical firm's curve → true.
R: market quantity at each price is the sum of all firms' quantities → true.
Adding n identical curves multiplies the quantity response by n, making the curve flatter.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks market supply has the same slope as one firm's

quiz.q: Three firms supply 20, 35 and 45 units at ₹50. What is the market supply at ₹50?
steps: Market supply at a price = sum of all firms' quantities at that price.
So market supply = 100 units.
Answer: 100
quiz.mistake: Averages instead of adding

teach.ask: Gappu and his cousin both sell nests. 'If I start selling at ₹5 and my cousin at ₹8, what does the market supply look like?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Add our quantities at each price. Below ₹8 only I sell, so the curve kinks at ₹8!
teach.nudge: Good! How do we combine our supply curves? What happens at the price where my cousin starts selling?

revise.summary: Market supply is the horizontal summation of all firms' supply curves. Kinks appear where firms with different shut-down prices start producing, and more firms shift market supply to the right.
focus: Add firms' supplies at a given price
Explain kinks in the market supply curve
Calculate market supply with n identical firms
Know the effect of a change in the number of firms
remember: Market supply: at each price, add the quantities supplied by all firms
n identical firms: market supply = n × s(p)
traps: Add quantities, not prices
A firm supplies zero below its shut-down price: don't include negative quantities
Don't forget to multiply by the number of firms

learn.hook: When the price of cricket balls doubles before the IPL season, how quickly can Meerut's workshops raise output? Elasticity of supply measures that response.
points: Price elasticity of supply e_S = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price. It is positive because price and quantity supplied move together.
Percentage method: e_S = (ΔQ/Q) × (P/ΔP). Use it both to compute e_S and to predict new quantities: %ΔQ = e_S × %ΔP.
Geometric method for a straight-line supply curve: if it meets the price axis (positive price intercept), e_S > 1; if it passes through the origin, e_S = 1; if it meets the quantity axis, e_S < 1.
Perfectly elastic supply (e_S = ∞): horizontal supply curve. Perfectly inelastic supply (e_S = 0): vertical supply curve (e.g. fixed stock of tickets for a match).

example.q: Price of cricket balls rises from ₹100 to ₹120 and quantity supplied rises from 500 to 650. Find e_S.

learn.reallife: The number of seats in a stadium for a World Cup final is fixed: supply of tickets is perfectly inelastic, whatever the price.

quiz.q: Price rises from ₹100 to ₹120 and quantity supplied rises from 500 to 650. Find e_S.
steps: Answer: 1.5
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: Price of cricket balls rises from ₹10 to ₹30 and supply rises from 200 to 1,000. Find e_S.
steps: e_S = 2
Answer: 2
quiz.mistake: Uses the change in quantity alone

quiz.q: e_S = 0.5. Price rises by 20% and the current supply is 400 units. What is the new quantity supplied?
steps: Answer: 440
quiz.mistake: Applies the full 20% to quantity

quiz.q: A straight-line supply curve passes through the origin. Its price elasticity at every point is:
quiz.explain: For q = bp, e_S = bp/q = 1.
steps: A line through the origin: q = bp.
e_S = (Δq/Δp) × (p/q) = b × p/(bp).
So e_S = 1 at every point.
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks the slope decides elasticity

quiz.q: A straight-line supply curve meets the price axis above the origin. Its elasticity is:
quiz.explain: For q = −a + bp with a > 0, e_S = bp/(bp − a) > 1.
steps: A line meeting the price axis above the origin: q = −a + bp with a > 0.
e_S = b × p/q = bp/(bp − a).
The denominator bp − a is smaller than bp.
So e_S > 1 (elastic).
Answer: Greater than 1
quiz.mistake: Swaps the price-axis and quantity-axis cases

quiz.q: The supply of tickets for a cricket final in a stadium with fixed seats is:
quiz.explain: Quantity cannot change whatever the price, so e_S = 0.
steps: The stadium has a fixed number of seats.
Whatever the price, the number of tickets cannot change.
Quantity not responding at all means e_S = 0.
So supply is perfectly inelastic.
Answer: Perfectly inelastic
quiz.mistake: Confuses perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Price elasticity of supply is generally positive.
Reason (R): Price and quantity supplied usually move in the same direction.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Same-direction movement makes the ratio positive.
steps: A: price elasticity of supply is generally positive → true.
R: price and quantity supplied usually move in the same direction → true.
Same-direction changes make the ratio positive.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Expects a negative sign as in demand

quiz.q: Supply q = 20 + p. Find e_S at p = 20.
quiz.explain: q = 40; e_S = (Δq/Δp) × p/q = 1 × 20/40 = 0.5 (line meets the quantity axis, so e_S < 1).
steps: Δq/Δp = 1
Answer: 0.5
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by p/q

teach.ask: Gappu's nest price rose from ₹10 to ₹12 and he raised output from 50 to 55 nests. 'How elastic is my supply?'
teach.praise: Tweet! %ΔQ = 10%, %ΔP = 20%, so e_S = 0.5: my supply is inelastic!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the percentage changes in quantity and price? Which do you divide by which?

revise.summary: Price elasticity of supply is the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price; it is positive. For straight-line supply curves, the axis the line meets tells whether e_S is greater than, equal to or less than 1.
focus: Calculate e_S by the percentage method
Predict new quantity supplied from e_S
Use the geometric method for straight-line supply curves
Know perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic supply
remember: e_S = (ΔQ/Q) × (P/ΔP)
Line meets price axis: e_S > 1; through origin: e_S = 1; meets quantity axis: e_S < 1
Perfectly elastic: horizontal; perfectly inelastic: vertical
traps: Don't invert the ratio: %ΔQ is on top
Elasticity of supply is positive, not negative as in demand
Don't swap the price-axis and quantity-axis cases
